## Maps

These maps show two different approaches to depicting Greenland. The left map is an orthographic projection, emulating a globe. The right map is a Mercator projection, which exaggerates the sizes of landmasses — including Greenland — that are closest to the poles.

## Introduction to Spatial Data

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
We are going to build geographic maps in R. To do this, we work with spatial vectors.

Standard dataframes hold text and numbers. Spatial dataframes hold geometries:

-   **Points:** A specific animal sighting or a single tree.
-   **Lines:** Rivers, roads, or animal movement tracks.
-   **Polygons:** State boundaries, lakes, or oceans.

(Why do paper maps never win at poker?

Because they always fold).
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/clipboard-211788351.png)
:::
:::::

## The Spatial Toolkit

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
To handle these geometries, we need libraries that bridge the gap between geographic data and the `tidyverse`.

-   `sf` (Simple Features): backbone of R spatial analysis. It makes maps act like dataframes.
-   `tigris`: Pulls accurate US boundaries (states, counties) directly from the Census Bureau.
-   `rnaturalearth`: Provides global boundaries, including Canada, lakes, and oceans.
-   `rinat`: Pulls community-science observations directly from iNaturalist.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
# Install if needed:
# install.packages("sf")
# install.packages("tigris")
# install.packages("rnaturalearth")
# install.packages("rinat")
# install.packages("osmdata")

# load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tigris)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(rinat)
library(osmdata)   
```
:::
:::::

## Map Projections: Flattening the Earth

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
The Earth is a 3D sphere. Our screens are flat. A map projection is the mathematical formula used to flatten the Earth.

Every projection distorts something: - area, - shape, - distance, or - direction

In R, changing a projection means recalculating the underlying grid. We define projections using a Coordinate Reference System (CRS), often assigned via an EPSG code or a PROJ4 string. We ensure all our map layers share the exact same CRS so they align perfectly.
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/clipboard-2210289981.png)
:::
:::::

## Fetching the Base Map

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   First, we pull the political and physical boundaries. Filter data to the specific states/ provinces.
-   Use st_transform() to set a uniform projection.
-   Here, use EPSG 4269 (NAD83), which is standard for North American mapping.
-   USA Contiguous Albers Equal Area (EPSG: 5070) -preserves area so same all over
-   Lambert Conformal Conic (EPSG: 3857 or State-Specific)
-   MN/WI/IA: Mostly UTM Zone 15N (EPSG: 26915) - high res state specific
-   MI: Mostly UTM Zone 16N (EPSG: 26916)- high res state specific
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| paged-print: false
### US States
midwest <- states(cb = TRUE, resolution = "20m") %>% 
  filter(STUSPS %in% c("MN", "WI", "MI", "ND", "SD", "IA")) %>% 
  st_transform(crs = 4269)

### Canadian Provinces
canada <- ne_states(country = "Canada", returnclass = "sf") %>% 
  filter(name %in% c("Ontario", "Manitoba")) %>% 
  st_transform(crs = 4269)

### Major Lakes
lakes <- ne_download(scale = 50, type = "lakes", 
                     category = "physical", 
                     returnclass = "sf") %>% 
  st_transform(crs = 4269)
```
:::
:::::

## Fetching Fisher Data

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
Fishers (*Pekania pennanti*) are a key mustelid in Minnesota's forests.

We will query recent observations from iNaturalist using **rinat**.

The data comes in as a standard dataframe (latitude/longitude columns).

Use st_as_sf() to convert those columns into a recognized spatial point geometry.

![](images/clipboard-3990679598.png)
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
# Get iNaturalist data 
# black bear Ursus americanus
fisher_raw <- get_inat_obs(taxon_name = "Pekania pennanti ", 
                           bounds = c(40, -100, 50, -85), # lat lon
                           maxresults = 200)

# Convert to a spatial object
fisher_sf <- st_as_sf(fisher_raw, 
                      coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), 
                      crs = 4326) %>% # 4326 is standard GPS coordinates
  st_transform(crs = 4269) # Match the base map projection

```
:::
:::::

## Building the Map (Points)

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
Mapping in sf relies on geom_sf().

Stack layers exactly like a lasagna. Bottom layers first (land), top layers last (points).

We use coord_sf() to zoom the "camera lens" to our specific bounding box.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = canada, fill = "gray95", color = "gray50") +
  geom_sf(data = midwest, fill = "gray95", color = "gray50") +
  geom_sf(data = lakes, fill = "aliceblue", color = "lightblue") +
  geom_sf(data = fisher_sf, color = "darkred", size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-100, -85), ylim = c(40, 50), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Fisher Sightings in the Midwest",
       caption = "Data: iNaturalist")

```
:::
:::::

## Distribution Heatmaps

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
Points are great, but dense clusters become illegible. We can use a 2D kernel density estimate (a heatmap) to highlight distribution hotspots.

To use stat_density_2d(), we extract the raw coordinates back out of our spatial object, then map the calculated density (after_stat(level)) to a color gradient.
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
# Extract raw coordinates for the density function
fisher_coords <- fisher_sf %>%
  mutate(lon = st_coordinates(.)[,1],
         lat = st_coordinates(.)[,2]) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = canada, fill = "grey80", color = "grey50") +
  geom_sf(data = midwest, fill = "grey80", color = "grey50") +
  geom_sf(data = lakes, fill = "lightblue", color = NA) +
  stat_density_2d(data = fisher_coords, 
                  aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = after_stat(level)), 
                  geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-100, -85), ylim = c(40, 50), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Fisher Sighting Density",
       fill = "Density")
```
:::
:::::

## Making more maps with other features - streams

Get Minnesota State Boundary

```{r}
mn_base <- states(cb = TRUE, resolution = "500k") %>% filter(STUSPS == "MN")
```
## Get Lake Superior Boundary

```{r}
great_lakes <- ne_download(scale = 10, type = "lakes",
                           category = "physical", 
                           returnclass = "sf") 
lake_superior <- great_lakes %>% 
  filter(name == "Lake Superior")

# Match CRS (Crucial for spatial operations)
lake_superior <- st_transform(lake_superior, st_crs(mn_base))

# 3. Create a "Clipping Box" for the West Arm
# This creates a polygon of the area specifically around the NE tip
west_arm_box <- st_bbox(c(xmin = -92.5, ymin = 46.5, xmax = -89.0, ymax = 48.5), 
                        crs = st_crs(mn_base)) %>% 
                st_as_sfc()

# 4. Clip the lake to that specific box
lake_superior_clipped <- st_intersection(lake_superior, west_arm_box)
```

## Get the North Shore Rivers

```{r}
set_overpass_url("https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter") 

# Dynamic MN box (adds a small buffer to ensure edges aren't cut)
mn_bbox <- st_bbox(mn_base)

# Get Rivers
rivers_data <- opq(bbox = mn_bbox, timeout = 400) %>%
  add_osm_feature(key = "waterway", value = c("river")) %>% 
  osmdata_sf()

rivers <- rivers_data$osm_lines
```

## Match coordinate systems and clip exactly to the MN boundary

```{r}
# Match coordinate systems
mn_base_matched <- st_transform(mn_base, crs = st_crs(rivers))
# Clip/Filter to the MN boundary
rivers_mn <- st_filter(rivers, mn_base_matched)
```



## Map Generation
::::: columns
::: {.column width="100%"}
```{r}
rivers.plot <- ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = mn_base_matched, fill = "gray95", color = "gray50") + 
  geom_sf(data = lake_superior_clipped, fill = "aliceblue", color = "lightblue") +
  # geom_sf(data = inland_lakes_mn, fill = "#D4E6F1", color = "#85C1E9", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = rivers_mn, 
          color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.1) +
theme_minimal() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") + 
  coord_sf(crs = 26915) # to make minnesota look normal
rivers.plot 
```
:::
